findings.desc: Previously TagDevice ran in a fire-and-forget goroutine using context.Background() with a 2-minute timeout, so DB write latency and client disconnects did not affect the response. Also, the recover() safety net was removed — a panic in TagDevice now propagates to the request handler (though HTTP middleware likely catches it). Consider whether a detached context (e.g., context.WithoutCancel or Background+timeout) is more appropriate for a write that should persist regardless of client behavior.

With the caching tests gone, a future change that swaps `=== undefined` for `=== null` (which would rebuild filter conditions on every call, or skip caching of the null result) would not be caught. Please keep coverage for the caching behavior, including the null-result case.
findings.title: Caching tests removed while caching logic remains

findings.desc: The cancellation loop awaits each SendGrid request serially inside one try block, and only runs Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete) at the very end. If any single client.request throws (e.g. one bad/already-cancelled batch_id), control jumps to the catch and the collected prisma.workflowReminder.delete calls never execute. The already-cancelled reminders stay in the DB and get re-processed on the next cron run, re-attempting cancel against SendGrid for batches that may already be cancelled. Wrap each iteration's SendGrid call in its own try/catch so the DB row is always cleaned up.
findings.title: A single SendGrid cancel failure aborts all DB deletes

findings.desc: The deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder calls are invoked inside a forEach but their returned promises are never awaited and are no longer added to prismaPromises (the old code awaited the DB deleteMany via prismaPromises). On a serverless runtime the function can return/freeze right after `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` and res.send, so the `cancelled: true` update (email) or the row delete (SMS) may never complete. The result: a cancelled booking's email reminder is never marked cancelled and SendGrid still sends it. Collect these promises and await them before responding.
findings.title: Reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget, may not persist in serverless

findings.desc: In the reschedule handler, the previous booking's workflow reminders are cancelled via deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder inside a forEach whose returned promises are discarded (the old code awaited a deleteMany via Promise.all). The email path now only sets cancelled=true (deferred to the cron), and because the call isn't awaited the update may not persist before the tRPC handler returns in a serverless context. If it doesn't persist, the stale reminder for the now-cancelled old booking can still fire. Await these cancellations (collect the promises and Promise.all them) before proceeding, the same way handleCancelBooking should.
findings.title: Reschedule reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget

findings.desc: In checkIfIsAvailable's working-hours check, both `start` and `end` are derived from `slotStartTime`. The `end` variable is identical to `start`, so the `end > workingHour.endTime` condition compares the slot's *start* minute-of-day against the working hour end instead of the slot's end. This means a slot that starts within working hours but extends past workingHour.endTime is incorrectly treated as available, while a slot starting after workingHour.endTime would also be wrongly flagged only by start. `end` should use `slotEndTime`.
findings.title: Working hours end check uses slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

findings.desc: The whole-day-override special case compares two dayjs instances with `===`, which checks object reference equality and is always false for freshly constructed dayjs objects. This branch is therefore dead code and the intended all-day override handling never triggers. Use `.isSame()` for value comparison.
findings.title: dayjs objects compared with === (reference equality, always false)

findings.desc: The override day is computed as `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")`, where `dayjs(date.start)` interprets the Date in the server's *local* timezone, while the comparison target `slotStartTime` is `time.utc()` (UTC). The result therefore depends on the host server's local timezone rather than being deterministic. If the server is not in UTC, the day-matching (and thus availability) will be wrong. Both sides should be normalized to the organizer's timezone (e.g. `dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone)` and `dayjs.tz(time, organizerTimeZone)`) before comparing the day.
findings.title: Date-override day comparison mixes server-local and UTC day formatting

findings.desc: The offset `inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` is derived from `override.start` and then reused for `override.end`. Around a DST transition the organizer/invitee UTC offset can differ between start and end of the same override, so the end time can be shifted by the wrong amount. Consider computing the offset independently for `override.end` as well.

findings.desc: The computed property keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` do NOT create catch-all / passthrough entries as the comments imply. `z.string()` returns a ZodType instance whose Object.prototype.toString is "[object Object]", so both keys collapse to the literal string "[object Object]" (the second overwriting the first). The resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() }`. Because zod objects strip unknown keys by default, every field other than access_token (e.g. expiry_date, expires_in, scope, token_type, refresh_token) is dropped from the parsed output. This is a real bug: callers like Google's CalendarService set `googleCredentials.expiry_date` *before* calling parseRefreshTokenResponse, then persist the parsed `key` — so expiry_date is stripped and never stored, defeating the isExpired check and forcing a refresh on every call. The schema also never validates that any numeric expiry field ex…
findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys don't act as catch-all

findings.desc: The handler processes any HTTP method (GET, PUT, DELETE, etc.). There is no `req.method` check before parsing the body. A GET/DELETE with no body will hit `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` with `undefined`, which throws an unhandled ZodError and surfaces as a 500 (potentially leaking a stack trace) instead of a clean 405. Webhooks that mutate credentials should be POST-only. Add a method guard at the top of the handler.
findings.title: Webhook handler has no HTTP method restriction

findings.desc: The webhook secret is compared with `!==`, which is a non-constant-time comparison and theoretically susceptible to timing attacks that could recover the secret byte-by-byte. Since this header gates write access to user credentials, prefer a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` over equal-length Buffers, with a length check up front). Also note `req.headers` are lowercased by Node/Next; if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` is configured with mixed case it will silently never match and every request will be rejected.
findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time operator

findings.desc: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...))` will throw (and bubble to a 500) if the encrypted payload is malformed or the decryption key is mismatched. Likewise `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws an unhandled ZodError on an invalid body. For an externally-callable webhook that writes credentials, these should be caught and returned as a structured 400 so callers get a clear error and no stack trace is leaked.
findings.title: JSON.parse / symmetricDecrypt not wrapped in try-catch

The finding correctly identifies an additional real issue: without a req.method guard, non-POST requests (or requests without a body) can trigger a thrown parse error and should return 405 instead.

This is a legitimate security/robustness suggestion not covered by the golden set.

findings.desc: The new OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method` filter, unlike the original deleteMany which only targeted SMS reminders. The `retryCount` column is shared across ALL WorkflowReminder methods (SMS, EMAIL, etc.) on the same model. This SMS cron job will therefore delete EMAIL (or any other method) reminders whose retryCount exceeds 1, even though only this SMS scheduler increments retryCount today. The intent of the cleanup is clearly SMS-only, so the retry branch should be scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to avoid deleting reminders of unrelated methods if retryCount is ever set elsewhere.
findings.title: deleteMany retryCount branch not scoped to SMS method

findings.desc: The retry-increment logic lives only in the `else` (scheduledSMS falsy) and `catch` branches. When `message` is empty/null or `sendTo` is missing, the `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` block is skipped entirely, so neither `scheduled` is set nor `retryCount` incremented. The reminder stays `scheduled: false` and will be re-selected on every cron run for the full 7-day window, never hitting the retry cap and never being marked done. Consider incrementing retryCount (or marking scheduled) in this no-op path so such reminders eventually stop being processed.
findings.title: Reminders with empty message or missing sendTo are retried indefinitely

findings.desc: Both failure paths use `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, a read-then-write based on the value fetched at the start of the run. If two cron invocations overlap (or the same reminder is processed concurrently), both can read the same retryCount and write back the same incremented value, losing a retry count and potentially never reaching the `gt: 1` deletion threshold. Prefer Prisma's atomic `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` to make the increment safe under concurrency.
findings.title: retryCount increment is non-atomic read-modify-write

findings.desc: The variable is named `isTeamAdminOrOwner` but the logic requires the user to be BOTH an admin AND an owner (`&&`). Looking at the helper definitions, `isTeamAdmin` returns true for ADMIN or OWNER roles, while `isTeamOwner` only returns true for OWNER. So `isTeamAdmin && isTeamOwner` is only ever true for team OWNERS — team ADMINS are incorrectly denied the ability to add guests. The sibling confirm.handler.ts uses the correct OR semantics (`role === OWNER || role === ADMIN`). This should be `||` so that either admins or owners are permitted.
findings.title: isTeamAdminOrOwner uses && instead of || — only owners can add guests

findings.desc: `blacklistedGuestEmails` is built by lowercasing each entry from `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS`, but the comparison `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` uses the original-cased `guest` from the input (the schema only runs `z.string().email()`, no lowercasing). A guest email like `Spam@Example.com` will never match a blacklisted `spam@example.com`, defeating the blacklist. The same case-sensitivity flaw affects the existing-attendee dedup check (`guest === attendee.email`), allowing a duplicate attendee to be created by simply changing the email casing. Normalize the guest email to lowercase before both comparisons.
findings.title: Blacklist check is case-sensitive — uppercase guest emails bypass it

findings.desc: `handleAdd` sets `setIsInvalidEmail(true)` when validation fails, but never sets it back to `false` on a successful validation/mutation. If a user enters an invalid email, sees the error, then corrects it and clicks Add again, the red "emails must be unique/valid" message stays visible alongside the loading spinner and even after the success toast. The flag is only cleared by the Cancel button. It should be reset to `false` (or derived from the validation result) when validation passes before mutating.
findings.title: isInvalidEmail never reset on retry — stale error persists after fixing input

This makes delivery failures invisible to monitoring and impossible to diagnose. At minimum, log the error object (e.g. `console.error("Error sending AddGuestsEmails", err)`) so failures are diagnosable.
findings.title: sendAddGuestsEmails silently swallows all email send errors
